messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Ricardo Reyes was sixty-two years old, a psychiatrist who had built a respected practice in a Midwestern city after fleeing his native Chile in the late 1980s. For thirty years, he had treated others’ trauma while keeping his own sealed away. That changed one Tuesday afternoon when a patient—a veteran with PTSD—began describing the sound of boots on concrete. Ricardo felt his chest tighten. The air in the room seemed to vanish. He excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and stood gripping the sink as the memory returned without warning: the detention center, the fluorescent lights, the incomprehensible chatter of guards speaking rapid Spanish he could not parse because they were from a different region, their words a blur of accusation and mockery. Some moments of those weeks were excruciatingly clear—the smell of diesel, the cold metal chair—while others were complete blanks, as if his mind had simply erased them. When the memory came back, it felt completely real across all his senses at once, as though he were still there.

That evening, Ricardo turned on the news and saw a report about a military parade in Santiago. The images of uniformed men brought the same visceral response. He had come to believe that the institutions meant to protect him—the courts, the international human rights bodies—had let him down completely. The officers who had tortured him faced no consequences. They had retired with pensions. This conviction hardened into something permanent: the world was not safe, and no one would intervene. After that night, any news report about Chile, any glimpse of a uniformed figure on television, or even the sudden sound of rapid, unfamiliar Spanish chatter in a grocery store aisle could instantly bring the full memory back. He began to avoid going out after dark, then during the day. He rehearsed what to say before every interaction, running through possible questions and his answers, because he was certain that if he were caught off guard, the memory would overwhelm him and he would appear broken in front of others. At work, he found himself redirecting his thoughts whenever a patient mentioned authority or injustice, thinking of something else to keep the images at bay. But the more he did this, the more the memories seemed to lie in wait, triggered by smaller and smaller cues—a certain shade of green on a uniformed security guard, a news headline about Latin America.

The cycle tightened. Each time a trigger brought the memory back, Ricardo’s belief that the world was indifferent to his suffering grew stronger. And each time he rehearsed conversations or avoided going out, he felt more disconnected from the community he had once cherished. The loss of connection to his culture and community became a quiet grief he carried everywhere. He stopped attending the local Chilean cultural center; the sight of the flag made his stomach turn. He found himself scanning faces on the street for anyone in uniform, monitoring his environment so constantly that he could not focus on his patients’ words. The very profession that had given him purpose now felt like a minefield. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three weeks ago: a new patient, a young man in military fatigues, walked into his office for an intake. Ricardo felt the room tilt. He made an excuse, cancelled the session, and sat in his car for an hour, shaking. He was most afraid that he would lose his ability to work, that the one identity he had left—being a doctor—would be stripped away. What he hoped for, though he could barely say it aloud, was that someone might finally see him, not as a colleague or a survivor, but as a man who had been waiting thirty years for the world to acknowledge what had been done to him.
